chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah from one of the two Imams (peace be upon them) said:

Any woman or man who is in a hurry and departs from al-Mash'ar al-Haram at night, there is no harm; let him throw the Jamarah, then proceed, and order someone to sacrifice on his behalf. The woman shortens her hair and the man shaves it, then let him perform Tawaf with the House and with al-Safa and al-Marwah, then let him return to Mina. If he arrives at Mina and no sacrifice has been made for him, there is no harm if he sacrifices himself. He should carry his hair when he shaves in Mecca to Mina, and if he wishes, he may shorten (his hair) if he had performed Hajj before that.

key_terms.الصَّفَا وَالْمَرْوَةِ: Al-Safa and Al-Marwah (the hills for Sa'i)
key_terms.الْجَمْرَةَ: The Jamarah (the stone pillar at Mina)
key_terms.الْمَشْعَرِ الْحَرَامِ: Al-Mash'ar al-Haram (the Sacred Monument, i.e., Muzdalifah)
key_terms.لْيَطُفْ بِالْبَيْتِ: Let him perform Tawaf with the Kaaba

ai.seo_question: What are the steps and rulings for a pilgrim who leaves Muzdalifah at night during Hajj?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the fiqh of *Afadh* (leaving Muzdalifah before midnight) for both men and women, emphasizing that the sequence of post-Muzdalifah rites—Jamarah, sacrifice, hair cutting, and Tawaf al-Qudum—is flexible rather than strictly sequential. It highlights the practical leniency granted to pilgrims, such as the option to delay the sacrifice until reaching Mina or to perform it via a proxy, reflecting the Shia scholarly emphasis on ease (*taysir*) in Hajj rituals. The narration also specifies gender-specific norms for hair grooming (shaving for men, trimming for women) while maintaining the core obligation of returning to Mina to complete the remaining rites.
